paras: The Crittenden County lynching rumors of July 1888 were two reports that a Black official had been lynched near Marion, Arkansas, during the expulsion of Black county officers from Crittenden County. The first, that legislator Sandy Odom had been hanged, was denied the next day, and the second, a wire dispatch that a Black county official had been hanged by a white mob at Marion, was called unfounded in Memphis. The wire version nonetheless ran in papers from Savannah to Montana, some of them under approving headlines.

In the weeks before, armed white men in Crittenden County had ordered a group of Black officeholders and other men to leave the county, among them County Judge Daniel W. Lewis and legislator "Sandy" Odom. Some thirty of the exiles were living in Memphis, and the Memphis Appeal had already dismissed earlier alarms from the county as a "foundationless scare."

On Sunday night, July 22, an Appeal reporter walking with Lewis in Memphis heard that the Rev. Nightingale had told his Beale Street congregation of a woman's report that a colored man's body had been found "swinging from a limb, with his throat cut." Lewis said the first impression was that the dead man was Odom, "but investigation proved it otherwise," while Harvey of the Watchman said a railroad agent had told him Odom was the victim, killed between Marion and Crawfordsville. The Appeal wired Edmundson and Crawfordsville, and neither place knew anything of a lynching.
On July 23 the Appeal's reporter went to Marion, and the paper reported the next day that Odom "has not been lynched" and had answered advice to leave the county with "I will leave."

On July 24 a Post-Dispatch special from St. Louis said one of the county's Black officials had been hanged by a mob at Marion the night before. Traveling Auditor Townsend of the Gulf road, arriving in Springfield, Missouri, said the victim was "one of the banished eighteen," seized while trying to enter the court house and hanged in the woods, but added that details were hard to get because Marion was under armed guard. In Little Rock a rumor named County Judge Lewis as the victim, but Governor Hughes had no confirmation and Sheriff Werner said Marion was quiet when he left it on the morning of July 23.

A Memphis dispatch of July 24 called the report of a lynching at Marion "unfounded," and the Appeal's editorial page called Townsend's statement "a falshood from beginning to end." No later report naming a victim, describing an inquest or recording an arrest appears in the coverage.

The Memphis Appeal, the nearest daily, both denied the lynching and mocked those who reported it, printing the Townsend dispatch under the heads "It Was Awful!" and "The Worst Kind of Bosh." Its denial came from a paper openly hostile to the exiles, whom it described as men "who would kill any territory they infest," and it printed Judge John McClure's remark that "They ought to have hung Lewis."

Elsewhere the wire ran on July 25 in the Savannah Morning News as "Crittenden's Race War," in the Richmond Dispatch, and in the Sacramento Record-Union, which placed Marion in Missouri and printed no denial. The Los Angeles Herald and the Wheeling Register carried the Memphis denial, the Herald printing it beside the Townsend report under the head "The Report Confirmed." Western papers kept the uncorrected story alive for days, the Wichita Eagle heading it "Only Seventeen Left," the Great Falls Tribune "A County Officer Lynched" on July 28, and the Fort Benton River Press "One of the Negro Official Conspirators Duly Lynched" on August 1. The Cleveland Gazette's account of the expulsions, in August, listed Lewis and Odom among the men driven out and reported no lynching.

Townsend's account was second-hand and named no victim, while the denials came from Memphis, where the Appeal's own reporter and the sheriff had left Marion before the night the hanging was said to have occurred. The Odom rumor is the better settled of the two, since the Appeal reported his own reply from Marion the day after it circulated.

bases: The episode is a reported mob hanging of a Black county official at Marion (A8, A7) and an earlier report that Sandy Odom had been lynched (A3), both denied in Memphis (A5, A6, A11); no killing is confirmed in the coverage.

A Post-Dispatch special and Traveling Auditor Townsend's second-hand account said a white mob hanged a Black county official at Marion (A8, A7), but no victim was confirmed, a Little Rock rumor naming Judge Lewis was unconfirmed (A7), and Memphis reports called the story unfounded (A6, A11); the earlier Odom rumor was explicitly denied (A5).
The wire report of a hanging (A8, A7) was denied by a Memphis dispatch and the Memphis Appeal (A11, A10, A6), and the Odom rumor was contradicted by Odom's own reply (A5).

accounts.gist: Crittenden exiles in Memphis heard, via a sermon, that a colored man's body had been found hanging with his throat cut; Lewis said it was first thought to be Sandy Odom but was not, while Harvey of the Watchman, citing a railroad agent, said Odom was the victim.

accounts.label: Post-Dispatch special and Townsend
accounts.gist: A negro county official, one of the banished eighteen, was seized by a white mob while trying to enter the Marion court house and hanged in the woods; Marion was under armed guard.

accounts.label: Little Rock rumor
accounts.gist: The whites had lynched County Judge Lewis the night before; the governor and sheriff had no confirmation.

accounts.label: Memphis denial
accounts.gist: A Memphis dispatch called the report unfounded; the Appeal called it a falsehood, said Odom was alive and Marion and Crawfordsville quiet.

framing.detail: The Memphis Appeal denied the lynching under heads like 'The Worst Kind of Bosh' and 'Peace in Crittenden' while calling the banished officials men 'who would kill any territory they infest' and printing a judge's remark that Lewis 'deserved to be hung'.
Most distant papers printed the Post-Dispatch and Townsend dispatches as fact under heads such as 'Crittenden's Race War' and 'A County Officer Lynched', some without the denial.
Some headline writers treated the reported hanging approvingly: 'Only Seventeen Left' (Wichita) and 'One of the Negro Official Conspirators Duly Lynched' (Fort Benton).

versions.value: A negro county official was hanged by a mob at Marion on the night of July 23.
The report is unfounded; Marion and Crawfordsville were quiet.

conflicts.note: Townsend's account was second-hand and named no victim; the Memphis denial is local, but the Appeal was openly hostile to the exiles, and its reporter and the sheriff had left Marion before the night in question (A7).

conflicts.note: Odom was reported alive on July 24 (A5); no report confirms any victim.
